accuracy.evidence: Checked against USGS This Dynamic Earth and the BGS plate tectonics pages: the lithosphere (crust plus rigid upper mantle) is broken into plates that move over the asthenosphere, which is solid rock that deforms and flows slowly, not liquid; plates move a few centimetres a year and the Atlantic widens about 2.5 cm a year (USGS compares this to fingernail growth), so 1 million years gives 25 km; divergent boundaries make new crust (Mid-Atlantic Ridge, Iceland); oceanic lithosphere is denser and subducts under continental lithosphere, forming trenches and volcanic arcs (Japan); continent-continent collision raised the Himalayas as India moved into Asia; the San Andreas Fault is a transform boundary that sticks and slips (elastic rebound) in earthquakes; Wegener's continental drift used the coastline fit and Mesosaurus fossils in Brazil and southern Africa; Pangaea broke up from about 200 million years ago. The cross-section labels the crust as drawn thicker than real, and the jigsaw shapes as simplified.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented alternative conceptions in Earth science education research (Libarkin and others; BGS teaching notes): plates float on a sea of liquid magma (step 1 predict, p1, challenge tag lava, adult text), plates move fast or not at all (step 2 predict, m2, tags fast and still), a hole opens when plates part (apart step message, tag hole), the continent sinks under the ocean plate (step 4 predict, p3, tag under), the Himalayas are volcanoes (tag volc, m4), sliding plates move smoothly (step 5 predict, p5, tag smooth), fossils matched because animals swam across (tag swim, m5), and earthquakes happen anywhere (tags middle and random, m6).

lab_distinct.evidence: gate_lab_distinct passed (under 30% similar to every flagship lab). 583 What Is an Earthquake mentions plates in one line and is about shaking and safety; 912 is about seismometers; 560 volcanoes; 724 Ring of Fire maps where earthquakes and volcanoes cluster and names plates in one paragraph, but has no layers, speeds, boundary mechanisms or drift evidence. This lab is about plate motion itself: a tappable cut-away Earth, a years dial that converts 2.5 cm a year into a gap, slabs that are dragged apart over rising magma, an ocean slab that bends down under a continent before a second pair crumples into a mountain, a locked fault whose road bends with strain then breaks at the fault line on each jolt, a jigsaw where both continents share one coastline so they fit only one way, and a five-place boundary sort.

lab_teaches.evidence: Children see the result before the text names it: the gap grows from 2.5 cm to 25 km only as the dial reaches a million years; magma fills the crack and grey stripes of new rock build on both sides as they drag; the ocean plate visibly bends and slides under the continent and a trench and volcano appear; the road bends while the strain bar fills and then snaps to an offset at the fault, so the stick-slip idea is felt twice; the fossils on both coasts line up only when the shapes touch. The boundary sort then applies all three types to real places.

predictions.evidence: Step 1 asks what is under the plates with 'a sea of runny lava' tempting; the mantle label and feedback say solid rock that flows slowly. Step 2 asks how fast plates move with 'about as fast as a car' and 'they never move' tempting; the dial shows 2.5 cm a year. Step 4 asks which plate goes under with 'the continent plate' tempting; the ocean slab sinks. Step 5 asks how sliding plates move with 'smoothly, a little each day' tempting; the strain bar and jolts disprove it.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Every distractor in the eight challenge questions has its own tag and message in plate_art.js WHY: lava, core, fast, still, hole, mount, under, bounce, apartm, volc, newfloor, smooth, swim, luck, middle and random. In the lab, a wrong layer tap names the layer tapped and what it is, and each wrong boundary pick names the slip ('Not pushing together: at Iceland there is no crumpling or sinking plate. Look for a crack that widens or rocks sliding sideways.').

readability.evidence: learn/readability.py gives the kid text grade 2.9 (limit 6.5) and the adult text 8.0 (limit 9.5). Kid sentences are short and concrete ('It is solid rock that can flow very, very slowly, like stiff putty.'); the precise terms for the age band (crust, mantle, core, tectonic plate, plate boundary, divergent, convergent, transform, subduction, trench, fault, continental drift, Pangaea) are in the key idea and adult text.

no_filler.evidence: gate_content found no filler phrases. Each kid paragraph matches lab steps (layers, mantle and speed, the three boundary types, the jigsaw evidence); the adult text gives the curriculum links, what each of the seven steps does and the named mistakes; every hint points to a specific dial, label or step in the lab.

After the first pass the head text was made light on the dark-theme banner, the subducting slab was moved below a thinner continent so it shows in the mantle, the Himalayas label was moved off the banner, the fault road now bends with strain and breaks at the fault after a jolt, and the South America label is clamped so it is not clipped at the left edge. accessibility.evidence: gate_browser passed: axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13, all 7 tasks complete with Show me, no console errors. Every canvas action has a button (Tap the crust/mantle/outer core/inner core, Fewer/More years, Pull the plates apart, Push them back, Push the plate, Move South America closer, Pulling apart/Pushing together/Sliding past), and the canvas aria-label is rewritten after each action with the layer, years and gap, how far apart or pushed the plates are, the strain and jolt count, the distance between the coasts, and the place being sorted.
